Identify the differential equation that generated the slope field above.
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069297/assets/f26e5b61c573664f0397667aff82cfe5d918e0d22f005658862c28c53d5de748.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the solution curves have vertical asymptotes $x=2$ and $x=4.$

Of the given equations, the only two that satisfy this condition are

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}=\frac{1}{(x-2)(x-4)}
$$

 
and

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}=\frac{{x}^{4}}{(x-2)(x-4)}.
$$

- Second, the slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $x\to \pm \infty .$ 

Of the two remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}.
$$

Notice that

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}\to 0\,\text{as}\,x\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}$ become horizontal as $x\to \pm \infty .$

On the other hand,

$$
\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{(1-\frac{6}{x}+\frac{8}{{x}^{2}})}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}$ do *not* become horizontal as $x\to \pm \infty .$
